power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Mobilizing Family and Community Cultural Wealth for Heritage Language Maintenance: Insights from Community-Based Talleres

text.text: Background: Heritage-language maintenance is shaped not only by family language practices but also by broader social and community contexts.

This study examined how participants in community-based talleres (workshops) described the resources they used to support bilingualism and heritage-language maintenance, using Community Cultural Wealth (CCW; Yosso, 2005) as the primary framework.
Methods: Four community-based talleres were held at a public library in a highly multicultural area of San Diego, California.
Participants included 23 individuals ranging from families, youth, educators, and community members.

Data included facilitator field notes analyzed using a CCWguided qualitative approach alongside inductively identified themes, as well as pre-and postworkshop survey responses summarized descriptively.

Results: Participants described heritage-language maintenance as extending beyond homelanguage use to include literacy, extended-family relationships, cultural activities, educational opportunities, community resources, social networks, and cross-border connections.
Linguistic, familial, social, navigational, aspirational, and resistant capital operated as interconnected resources.
Participants also described tensions surrounding correction, "proper" Spanish, and linguistic legitimacy.
Survey responses were generally favorable at baseline, with shifts in beliefs about school-language difficulties and caregiver expertise.
The talleres functioned as reciprocal spaces in which community knowledge contextualized and sometimes reshaped research-based recommendations.
Heritage-language maintenance emerged as an ecological and relational process shaped by family and community resources, opportunities for meaningful language use, and linguistic legitimacy.
Community-2 engaged approaches may be most effective when they recognize families, external community networks as knowledge holders and avoid overly prescriptive recommendations.

Gloria Anzaldúa (1999) described life in the borderlands as "living on borders and in margins, keeping intact one's shifting and multiple identity and integrity," an experience she compared to "trying to swim in a new element, an 'alien ' element" (p. 19).
text.formatted: Gloria <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Anzaldúa (1999)</ref> described life in the borderlands as "living on borders and in margins, keeping intact one's shifting and multiple identity and integrity," an experience she compared to "trying to swim in a new element, an 'alien <ref type="bibr">' element" (p. 19)</ref>.

text.text: Rooted in the U.S.-Mexico border, Anzaldúa's borderlands describe spaces where languages, cultures, identities, and systems of power intersect.
Bilingual families navigate these intersections across homes, schools, communities, and institutions, where languages serve different functions and carry unequal social value.
Heritage-language maintenance must be understood within the broader social conditions that shape language use across contexts and generations.
These conditions are relevant in the linguistically diverse United States.
In 2025, approximately 74.2 million U.S. residents aged five and older spoke a language other than English at home, including nearly 45 million Spanish speakers (U.S. Census Bureau, 2025).
Although home-language use is not equivalent to bilingual proficiency, these estimates underscore the scale of multilingualism in the United States.
Yet demographic diversity does not correspond to equal institutional support for multilingualism.
English remains dominant across many educational and public contexts.

U.S. bilingual education has historically alternated between additive approaches that support continued bilingual development and transitional approaches that use the home language primarily to facilitate English acquisition. Gándara (2018) describes how bilingual education was often framed as a response to linguistic disadvantage rather than as a means of sustaining bilingualism and biliteracy.
text.formatted: U.S. bilingual education has historically alternated between additive approaches that support continued bilingual development and transitional approaches that use the home language primarily to facilitate English acquisition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gándara (2018)</ref> describes how bilingual education was often framed as a response to linguistic disadvantage rather than as a means of sustaining bilingualism and biliteracy.

text.text: Under such models, the home language functioned as a bridge to English rather than as an enduring educational resource.
These tensions are salient in California, where 44.4% of residents age five and older reported speaking a language other than English at home between 2020 and 2024 (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.).
Spanish-English bilingualism is widespread, but bilingual experiences vary by migration history, generation, geography, family language practices, schooling, and opportunities for use.

This variation challenges accounts of U.S. Spanish centered on language loss or deviation from monolingual norms and instead points to the heterogeneity of bilingual experience (Amengual et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This variation challenges accounts of U.S. Spanish centered on language loss or deviation from monolingual norms and instead points to the heterogeneity of bilingual experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Amengual et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: California's location along the U.S.-Mexico border adds another dimension to this linguistic ecology.
Border-region contexts can create opportunities for movement across linguistic, familial, and cultural networks.

For example, Brochin Ceballos (2012) found that transnational experiences supported Spanish biliteracy and bicultural identities among bilingual teachers who had limited access to additive bilingual education.
text.formatted: For example, Brochin <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Ceballos (2012)</ref> found that transnational experiences supported Spanish biliteracy and bicultural identities among bilingual teachers who had limited access to additive bilingual education.

text.text: These experiences can expand opportunities for heritage-language use, but proximity to the border alone does not ensure maintenance.
Continued transmission depends on sustained opportunities to use and develop the heritage language across family, school, and community contexts.

The present study takes a community-centered approach to engage directly with families and community members to better understand their experiential knowledge about the linguistic needs of their children and the resources available within their communities in maintaining their heritage languages.

text.text: Heritage languages are minoritized languages learned early through family and community interaction in settings where another language typically dominates schooling and public life (Montrul, 2023; Rothman, 2009).

text.text: In the United States, this often produces an intergenerational pattern in which immigrant adults primarily use the heritage language (e.g., Spanish), their children become bilingual, and later generations progressively use English more (Alba et al., 2002; Potowski, 2013; Portes & Hao, 1998 , 2002).
text.formatted: In the United States, this often produces an intergenerational pattern in which immigrant adults primarily use the heritage language (e.g., Spanish), their children become bilingual, and later generations progressively use English more <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alba et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Potowski, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Portes & Hao, 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Language maintenance depends on continued transmission from one generation to the next and on opportunities to use the language beyond early childhood (Pascual y Cabo & Gómez Soler, 2015; Potowski, 2013).
text.formatted: Language maintenance depends on continued transmission from one generation to the next and on opportunities to use the language beyond early childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pascual y Cabo & Gómez Soler, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Potowski, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: School entry can change these linguistic opportunities.
Children who have used Spanish at home may begin spending much of the day learning, reading, and interacting with peers in English.
As English use expands across settings, opportunities to hear and produce Spanish may become concentrated within the home.

Research with Spanish-English bilinguals shows that changes in the relative amount of input and use in each language are important for Spanish development (Bohman et al., 2010; Hoff & Core, 2013; Montanari et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Research with Spanish-English bilinguals shows that changes in the relative amount of input and use in each language are important for Spanish development <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bohman et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hoff & Core, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Montanari et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, English schooling does not necessarily produce immediate Spanish loss: Montanari and colleagues (2025) found continued growth in Spanish during children's first year of English-only preschool in Los Angeles, although outcomes varied with children's experiences and maternal cultural orientation.

text.text: Sustained instruction in Spanish can provide additional opportunities for development (Cabrera Pérez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Sustained instruction in Spanish can provide additional opportunities for development <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cabrera Pérez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Among school-age Spanish-English bilingual children, Montrul and Potowski (2007) found no evidence of increasing language loss with age among students enrolled in a dual-immersion program, suggesting that heritage-language schooling can support continued development.
text.formatted: Among school-age Spanish-English bilingual children, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Montrul and Potowski (2007)</ref> found no evidence of increasing language loss with age among students enrolled in a dual-immersion program, suggesting that heritage-language schooling can support continued development.

text.text: Opportunities beyond school are also important for heritage-language maintenance.

Heritage-language maintenance is associated with regular use with parents and extended family, access to other speakers, literacy and media experiences, social networks, and institutional support (Albudoor et al., 2025; DeCapua & Wintergerst, 2009; Potowski, 2013).
text.formatted: Heritage-language maintenance is associated with regular use with parents and extended family, access to other speakers, literacy and media experiences, social networks, and institutional support <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Albudoor et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">DeCapua & Wintergerst, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Potowski, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Community context can expand these opportunities. Potowski (2013), for example, reviews evidence that greater concentrations of heritage-language speakers and proximity to regions where the language is widely used are associated with greater maintenance.
text.formatted: Community context can expand these opportunities. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Potowski (2013)</ref>, for example, reviews evidence that greater concentrations of heritage-language speakers and proximity to regions where the language is widely used are associated with greater maintenance.

text.text: At the same time, the demographic presence of Spanish does not ensure its transmission: continued immigration may sustain Spanish at the population level even when individual families shift toward English across generations.
These findings also caution against equating bilingual variation with language loss.

Heritage speakers differ in when, where, and with whom they use each language, and these differences shape vocabulary, grammar, literacy, and patterns of language choice. Higby et al. (2023) argue that evaluating such outcomes against monolingual norms can position expected bilingual variation as deficiency.

(2023)</ref> argue that evaluating such outcomes against monolingual norms can position expected bilingual variation as deficiency.

text.text: The distinction is important for family bilingualism: reduced use of Spanish in some settings may indicate changing language opportunities, but it does not by itself demonstrate that a child has lost the language.
Continued heritage-language use can also sustain communication with parents and extended family and preserve access to broader social networks (DeCapua & Wintergerst, 2009; Gándara, 2018).
text.formatted: Continued heritage-language use can also sustain communication with parents and extended family and preserve access to broader social networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(DeCapua & Wintergerst, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gándara, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Such relational functions are especially relevant to the present study because participants frequently described bilingualism in terms of intergenerational communication, family connection, and future transmission.
Heritage-language maintenance depends not only on family intentions but also on families' access to, and ability to create or navigate, opportunities for meaningful language use.
This distinction shifts attention from individual language choices toward the social and institutional resources that make those choices possible.
Opportunities to use Spanish are only one condition for heritage-language maintenance.
Speakers also encounter judgments about what counts as "correct" Spanish and who is considered a competent Spanish speaker.
Heritage bilinguals are often evaluated against monolingual or standardized norms that do not reflect their histories of exposure and use (Higby et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Heritage bilinguals are often evaluated against monolingual or standardized norms that do not reflect their histories of exposure and use <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Higby et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, essentialist categories such as native speaker can obscure variation in language experience and position some speakers as more legitimate than others (Namboodiripad et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, essentialist categories such as native speaker can obscure variation in language experience and position some speakers as more legitimate than others <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Namboodiripad et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These judgments are not socially neutral.

Raciolinguistic research shows that perceptions of language are shaped by broader perceptions of speakers and their racialized identities (Flores & Rosa, 2015; Rosa, 2016; Rosa & Flores, 2017). Flores and Rosa (2015), for example, argue that racialized speakers can continue to be perceived as linguistically deficient even when they approximate standardized forms. Rosa (2016) similarly describes how U.S. Latine speakers may be positioned as deficient in English while also being characterized as speakers of inadequate Spanish.

text.text: These frameworks help explain why greater conformity to a prescribed standard does not necessarily eliminate linguistic stigma.

For U.S. heritage Spanish speakers, these ideologies often appear through expectations to speak a standardized or "proper" variety. Lynch and Potowski (2014) argue that prescriptive approaches to U.S. Spanish can devalue bilingual practices and undermine efforts to sustain Spanish.

text.text: More recent research documents similar patterns in educational settings. Johnson et al. (2024) found that Spanish heritage-language students can encounter programs organized around monolingual norms and standard-language ideologies that privilege traditional second-language learners while marginalizing U.S. Spanish varieties.

text.text: Research with Southern California Spanish-English bilinguals also show awareness of stigma attached to contact-influenced forms and English borrowings associated with local bilingual Spanish (Holguín Mendoza & Higby, 2024).

text.text: The label no sabo kid illustrates how these ideologies operate in U.S. heritage-Spanish contexts.

The term has been documented as a deficit-oriented and derogatory label for heritage speakers whose Spanish is perceived as insufficiently proficient, potentially reinforcing linguistic insecurity rather than encouraging continued use (Johnson et al., 2024; McKinnon, 2026a McKinnon, , 2026b)).

Gándara (2018) notes that bilingual programs historically framed as compensatory services for minoritized students have been sought as enrichment opportunities by English-dominant families.

text.text: Thus, bilingualism may be treated as an asset for some speakers while heritage bilingual practices remain subject to correction or deficit framing.

Supporting heritage-language maintenance requires attention not only to how often families use Spanish, but also to whether children and families experience their bilingual practices as legitimate resources.
Asset-based frameworks shift attention from presumed family deficits toward the knowledge and resources families already mobilize.
Funds of Knowledge (Moll et al., 1992) conceptualizes households as sites of historically-accumulated and culturally-developed knowledge.

text.text: Caregivers and community networks possess practical, cultural, and relational expertise that children draw on across contexts.

Applied to bilingualism, these resources may include knowledge of children's language preferences, strategies for encouraging use, literacy practices, media, family relationships, and opportunities for interaction.
Community Cultural Wealth (CCW; Yosso, 2005) extends this orientation by identifying resources that institutions often fail to recognize.
text.formatted: Community Cultural Wealth (CCW; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Yosso, 2005)</ref> extends this orientation by identifying resources that institutions often fail to recognize.

text.text: Yosso describes six interconnected forms of capital: aspirational, linguistic, familial, social, navigational, and resistant.

Linguistic capital encompasses skills developed through multiple languages and communicative styles; familial capital reflects knowledge and support transmitted through kinship networks; social capital involves access to people and community resources; navigational capital concerns movement through institutions; aspirational capital reflects hopes sustained despite barriers; and resistant capital includes knowledge and practices that challenge inequality.
Funds of Knowledge and CCW shift attention from what families are presumed to lack toward the knowledge, relationships, linguistic practices, and navigational resources they already mobilize.

Applied to heritage-language maintenance, this perspective highlights how families draw on household knowledge, kinship ties, community networks, and institutional navigation while responding to language ideologies and unequal access to resources.
This asset-based orientation also changes how community support is conceptualized: if families are knowledge holders, outreach should not be limited to transmitting expert recommendations.
Research-based knowledge can instead be placed in dialogue with families' experiential knowledge, goals, and available resources.

Drawing on Yosso's (2005) CCW framework, we propose a conceptual framework (Figure 1) that situates heritage-language maintenance within the broader sociolinguistic ecology of the U.S.-Mexico border region.

text.text: Rather than viewing language maintenance solely as a product of individual family choices, this framework considers how family language practices are shaped by the interaction of community resources, institutional conditions, and transnational experiences.

This framework also acknowledges the barriers that families encounter and the linguistic, familial, social, and other forms of community cultural wealth that are drawn upon to support intergenerational language transmission.
In doing so, the framework also provides an asset-based lens for examining how families navigate both the opportunities and constraints of raising bilingual families in a border-region context.

Community-engaged approaches emphasize local knowledge, reciprocal learning, and collaboration rather than one-way dissemination. Vaughn et al. (2018) argue that community members contribute contextual knowledge, shared experience, cultural understanding, and social connections that can improve the relevance of research and educational initiatives.

text.text: This orientation is relevant to bilingual families because language practices vary across children, schools, communities, and linguistic environments.
Research can inform families about bilingual development, but families contribute knowledge about how language is used within specific relationships and contexts.
Neither source of knowledge alone captures the full ecology of bilingual development.
Community-based talleres (i.e., workshops) can bring these forms of knowledge into dialogue through discussion, case-based scenarios, and opportunities to exchange experiences and strategies.
Rather than prescribing a single approach to bilingualism, this model gives participants space to interpret research in relation to their own linguistic practices, goals, and resources.
This co-constructive orientation frames the workshops as sites of knowledge exchange rather than one-way instruction and provides the foundation for the present study.

Although research has documented family language practices, heritage-language shift, and the role of community resources, less attention has been given to how families' existing forms of cultural wealth become visible and are exchanged within community-based bilingualism outreach.

In particular, relatively little is known about how research-based information and family or community knowledge are negotiated in dialogic spaces where participants bring different linguistic histories, institutional experiences, and resources.

Examining these interactions can extend heritage-language maintenance research beyond descriptions of family practices to consider how knowledge and resources are collectively interpreted within community settings.
The present study examines a series of community-based bilingualism talleres conducted in a multilingual California border-region community.

Guided by Community Cultural Wealth (Yosso, 2005), we examine how participants described the resources and strategies they drew on to support bilingualism and heritage-language maintenance, and how the talleres created opportunities for participants' experiential knowledge to interact with research-based information.
text.formatted: Guided by Community Cultural Wealth <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Yosso, 2005)</ref>, we examine how participants described the resources and strategies they drew on to support bilingualism and heritage-language maintenance, and how the talleres created opportunities for participants' experiential knowledge to interact with research-based information.

text.text: The study addressed the following research questions: 1.
How do participants describe the practices, experiences, and resources they use to support bilingualism and heritage-language maintenance?
What forms of Community Cultural Wealth are reflected in these practices and experiences?
How is knowledge about bilingual development and heritage-language maintenance exchanged and negotiated within the community-based talleres?
We approached this study as multilingual researchers with personal and professional connections to bilingual communities.

The first author was born in Cuba, raised in Spain, and moved to the United States at age 16, where he learned English as a second language; his research and community-engaged work focus on bilingual and typical and atypical language development.

The second author is Mexican American and a Spanish heritage speaker whose experiences include frequent movement across the U.S.-Mexico border and maintaining family relationships across both countries.
Her work with bilingual young adults further informs her understanding of heritage-language use across educational, family, and transnational contexts.

text.text: The study was conducted through a series of four community-based bilingualism talleres at a public library in City Heights, San Diego, California.

The talleres took place on four consecutive Saturdays and were conducted mainly in Spanish, providing an accessible community space where families and other community members could discuss bilingual development, heritage-language maintenance, and strategies for supporting multilingualism.
City Heights provides a relevant setting for this work because of its linguistic and cultural diversity and its location within the broader San Diego-Tijuana border region.

In 2023, City Heights had an estimated population of 67,964, of whom approximately 49% were Hispanic, 20% White, 16% Asian or Pacific Islander, and 11% Black (San Diego Association of Governments [SANDAG], 2023).
text.formatted: In 2023, City Heights had an estimated population of 67,964, of whom approximately 49% were Hispanic, 20% White, 16% Asian or Pacific Islander, and 11% Black (San Diego Association of Governments <ref type="bibr">[SANDAG], 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The public library served as an established community resource where families could access educational materials, multilingual programs for children and adults, and opportunities for interaction outside formal school or clinical settings.
This setting was therefore well suited for talleres centered on the exchange of research-based information and participants' lived experiences with bilingualism.
A total of 23 participants participated across the four talleres.
Participants included parents and caregivers, children, adolescents, young adults, educators, and other community members.

Although many participants had connections to Spanish-English bilingualism, the group was linguistically diverse and also included individuals with connections to Vietnamese, Japanese, and other linguistic backgrounds.

Participants varied in their experiences with bilingualism: some were raising bilingual children, some were heritage-language speakers themselves, and others were interested in supporting multilingual development within their families or communities.
Participants were recruited through community outreach associated with the library and local networks.
Participation in the talleres was voluntary, and attendance varied across sessions.

The workshops were designed for community participation from individuals of all ages and with different bilingual experiences, hence enrollment was not restricted to a narrowly defined demographic group.
The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the University of California, Irvine Institutional Review Board (Protocol No.
A waiver of informed consent was approved for the use of data generated through the community-based talleres.

Adapted from the Charlas model described by Perez et al. (2023), the bilingualism series consisted of four community-based talleres, with each session addressing a different aspect of bilingual development and family language use.

text.text: Topics included: communication in two languages, common misconceptions about bilingualism and language disorders, bilingualism among children with disabilities, and strategies for supporting bilingual development at home and in the community.
Although the content varied across sessions, the talleres followed a common structure intended to combine research-based information with participants' experiences and group discussion.
Each taller began with an informal welcome and social period, followed by a brief facilitator-led presentation, and extended participant discussion.

Approximately 10 minutes were allocated for introductions and informal conversation, 20 minutes for presentation of the session topic, and at least 30 minutes for discussion, with additional time used for surveys, questions, activities, and sharing resources.

text.text: Interactive verdad o mito (truth-or-myth) activities were also used to introduce common beliefs about bilingualism-related topics (e.g., verdad o mito: exposure to multiple languages confuses children or interferes with English acquisition).
Participants first considered these statements based on their own knowledge and experiences, after which facilitators discussed relevant research and invited further conversation.
These activities were intended to make participants' existing understandings visible and provide opportunities to discuss areas of agreement, uncertainty, or disagreement.
Case-based scenarios, presented as ejemplos de la vida real (real-life examples), were another central component of the talleres.

Scenarios depicted situations that bilingual families might encounter, including a child beginning English-only schooling after primarily using Spanish at home, parents being advised to stop using the home language, a child becoming increasingly reluctant to speak Spanish, bilingual children mixing languages, and families seeking affordable resources for bilingual literacy.
Rather than presenting an immediate solution, facilitators invited participants to respond to the situation and share whether they had encountered similar experiences.

Participants discussed possible strategies, compared them with their own family experiences, and generated additional considerations before facilitators introduced research-based information and available community resources.
We served both as sources of research-based information and as moderators of discussion.
We encouraged participants to question, elaborate on, or contextualize the information presented and emphasized that language practices and strategies could differ across families.

Participant contributions naturally and frequently redirected or expanded the discussion by introducing examples from their own children, schooling experiences, family relationships, cross-border experiences, and language-learning histories.
The talleres were thus structured not simply as educational presentations but as spaces in which research-based information and community knowledge could be discussed together.
Data consisted of field notes of approximately 6800 words documenting participant discussions and interactions across the four talleres.
Following each session, facilitators recorded participants' questions, examples, family language experiences, responses to case-based activities, and strategies shared during group discussion.
Field notes also included our observations and reflections about recurring topics, contrasting perspectives, and issues that emerged during each session.
Participant comments were analyzed as documented in these notes; verbatim quotations were used only when the wording had been recorded directly.
A brief eight-item pre-and post-workshop survey documented participants' perspectives on bilingual development, home-language maintenance, and strategies for supporting bilingual children.

Seven statements were administered before and after the taller and addressed homelanguage exposure, continued use of the home language, language-learning practices, interpretation of school-language difficulties, caregiver expertise, classroom support for bilingualism, and home-language reading.
An eighth statement, administered only at post-survey, asked whether the taller increased participants' knowledge of bilingualism.
Responses used a three-option pictorial scale and were summarized descriptively as favorable, neutral, or unfavorable.
Pre-and post-workshop responses were linked using participant identifiers.
Written responses were included in the qualitative analysis when relevant to the research questions.
Closed-ended survey responses were summarized using frequencies and percentages.
Pre-post comparisons were based on participants with responses at both time points for each item.
We conducted a framework-guided qualitative analysis of the field notes and written responses across the four talleres.
Community Cultural Wealth (Yosso, 2005) served as the primary analytic framework.

text.text: The first stage of analysis involved repeated review of the dataset to identify segments describing family language practices, intergenerational relationships, community resources, educational experiences, aspirations for bilingualism, institutional navigation, and responses to deficit-oriented beliefs about bilingual language use.
We then applied deductive codes corresponding to Yosso's (2005) six forms of capital: linguistic, familial, social, navigational, aspirational, and resistant.

text.text: Coding was not treated as mutually exclusive; a single account could reflect multiple forms of capital when participants described interconnected resources or strategies.

For example, maintaining Spanish through relationships with grandparents could reflect both familial and linguistic capital, whereas seeking a dual-language program could reflect aspirational and navigational capital.
Alongside this deductive coding, we attended to patterns that emerged across participants and sessions that were not fully captured by the six categories.

These included tensions surrounding language correction and linguistic legitimacy, differences in language practices across children and generations, and instances in which participants expanded, questioned, or contextualized recommendations introduced by facilitators.
Codes and interpretations were refined through comparison across the four talleres, with attention to recurring patterns as well as differences across participants and workshops (Saldaña, 2009).

text.text: A final cross-session synthesis examined how the different forms of CCW operated together across the workshop series.

This analysis also considered moments in which participants connected case scenarios to their own experiences, generated strategies beyond those presented by facilitators, or brought family and community knowledge into dialogue with research-based information.
These instances informed our interpretation of the talleres as spaces for knowledge exchange and co-construction.
To strengthen the credibility of the analysis, we collaboratively reviewed coded excerpts, emerging patterns, and analytic interpretations.

Coding decisions were discussed and refined through consensus, and analytic memos were used to document developing interpretations and connections across workshops (Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Saldaña, 2009; Vanover et al., 2021).

text.text: For example, participants differed in how they approached correcting children's Spanish, responding to language mixing, and creating opportunities for heritage-language use.

Reflexivity was maintained throughout the analytic process by considering how our multilingual, migration, cross-border, and professional experiences shaped the questions brought to the data and the interpretation of participants' accounts.

Consistent with the study's asset-based orientation, we focused on the knowledge, strategies, relationships, and resources participants mobilized rather than evaluating their practices against a predetermined model of successful bilingualism.

Across sessions, participants described bilingualism as something sustained through everyday family routines, relationships, community resources, educational choices, and efforts to create meaningful opportunities for language use.
Linguistic, familial, social, navigational, aspirational, and resistant capital frequently operated together rather than as discrete forms of support.
Because forms of cultural wealth frequently overlap, the findings are organized around recurring patterns in participants' accounts rather than presented as six discrete CCW categories.
Participants most often described heritage-language maintenance through ordinary family practices rather than formal instruction alone.

Speaking Spanish at home, reading, listening to music, maintaining relationships with relatives, and creating opportunities for children to use the language were described as ways of sustaining bilingualism.

These practices reflected both linguistic capital, through continued access to and use of multiple linguistic resources, and familial capital, through the knowledge caregivers developed about how individual family members used language.
Parents emphasized that children within the same family did not necessarily respond to the same language practices in the same way.
One mother summarized this expertise directly: "Como padres, somos quienes mejor conocemos las necesidades lingüísticas de nuestros hijos" [As parents, we know our children's language needs best].
This perspective was reflected in how caregivers adjusted their strategies according to children's confidence, preferences, and patterns of language use.

During the first taller, for example, one mother contrasted her two children: her younger child continued speaking Spanish even when unsure whether he was saying something "correctly," whereas her older child at times avoided speaking when uncertain.
Rather than treating these differences as evidence that one child was more capable than the other, she described adapting how she encouraged each child to participate.
She also emphasized maintaining Spanish at home because of its importance for communication with relatives and connection to Mexican culture.
Her account illustrates how familial knowledge shaped language practices at the level of the individual child rather than through a single strategy applied uniformly across the household.
Literacy emerged as another family resource.
The same mother described how her older son had begun reading Spanish after encountering a book that interested him.
He was surprised by how easily he could read and by how quickly his reading improved.
In another session, a mother of five described creating her own reading materials when her children were young and working with them regularly.
Her approach differed across children because some were initially more willing than others to use Spanish.
Rather than applying a single family language strategy, she adapted her practices according to each child's interests, confidence, and willingness to participate.
These accounts positioned literacy not only as exposure to Spanish but as a resource families adapted to children's interests and engagement.
Similar patterns extended beyond parent-child interactions.
Young adults described intentionally strengthening their Spanish through relationships, workplaces, music, and other forms of repeated language use.

These accounts suggest that heritage-language development remained active into adulthood and was supported through the social relationships and environments in which Spanish became meaningful or necessary.
Across these accounts, bilingualism was maintained through relationships and repeated use rather than through a single prescribed family language policy.
Familial knowledge also shaped how parents modified strategies over time.
In one of the sessions, one mother explained that she had emphasized correction and Spanish practice more strongly with her older children but took a different approach with her youngest daughter.
When the daughter responded to her in English, the mother continued speaking Spanish without necessarily requiring a Spanish response.
She also enrolled her in a dual-language program and ballet folklórico, creating additional opportunities to connect language with cultural participation.
Such examples illustrate how families drew simultaneously on linguistic and familial resources while adapting their practices to individual children and changing circumstances.

These examples show how linguistic and familial capital operated together as families adjusted their practices in response to individual children, prior experiences, and changing opportunities for language use.
Participants also described language maintenance as dependent on opportunities extending beyond the immediate household.
Schools, libraries, community programs, workplaces, extended-family networks, and cross-border relationships created additional contexts in which bilingualism could be developed or sustained.
Social and navigational capital were especially visible when participants described how they located, created, or adapted to uneven access to these opportunities.
Cross-border relationships were prominent.
One adult participant described traveling frequently between San Diego and Tijuana during childhood to visit family and friends and to use Spanish.
He had also attended kindergarten in Tijuana before beginning first grade in the United States.
Looking back, he attributed differences between his own Spanish and that of his younger sisters partly to his greater time in Tijuana and more frequent use of Spanish with family.
During the discussion, he proposed extended stays in Mexico as one possible way for children with family connections there to experience greater immersion in Spanish.

His suggestion emerged from his own history rather than from the facilitators' initial recommendations, illustrating how transnational experience functioned as both a linguistic resource and a form of navigational knowledge that could be shared with other families.
Participants also described navigating institutional constraints within the United States.

In the final taller, one African American grandmother wanted her five-year-old granddaughter to learn Spanish through a dual-language program but reported that the child's elementary school did not offer one.

The discussion consequently shifted toward other possible resources, including bilingual library programming, Spanish-language books and media, and interactions with Spanish-speaking family and community members.
The public library itself functioned as a community resource by connecting families with bilingual materials, programming, and other opportunities for language use.
In this way, social capital could help families identify alternatives when preferred educational opportunities were unavailable.
The multilingual composition of the final session further expanded the range of community knowledge represented.

A Vietnamese participant brought her own professional and family experiences to a discussion of bilingual development, emphasizing the importance of considering the amount of input and output in each language, children's age and grade, and how much time they spent using each language.
A Japanese mother emphasized that teachers should respect students' cultural backgrounds when responding to bilingual families.

These contributions broadened the conversation beyond Spanish-English bilingualism and demonstrated that participants were not only seeking resources but also contributing knowledge that expanded the resources available within the group.
Community navigation therefore involved more than finding formal bilingual programs.
Participants described building language opportunities through family travel, cultural activities, workplaces, partners, libraries, media, and community relationships.
When formal opportunities were limited or unavailable, participants described combining family, social, and community resources to create alternative contexts for language use.
Social and navigational capital were thus closely connected: access to people and community networks often provided the information needed to identify or create opportunities for bilingualism.
Aspirational capital was evident in participants' repeated emphasis on maintaining or developing bilingualism for future generations.
These aspirations were not limited to parents currently raising bilingual children.
Young adults also discussed Spanish in relation to future relationships, families, and children, suggesting that heritage-language maintenance was understood as an intergenerational project.

One young woman who had grown up speaking Spanish described teaching the language to her boyfriend and emphasized that maintaining the home language would be important when they eventually had children.
Similarly, a young man who had become more intentional about practicing Spanish as an adult described teaching Spanish to his future children as an eventual goal.
His current practices, speaking with a bilingual partner and listening to Mexican music, were therefore connected to a longer-term aspiration for intergenerational transmission.
Parents expressed similar aspirations even when access to resources was uneven.
One English-monolingual mother wanted her five-year-old daughter to become bilingual despite neither parent being a Spanish speaker.
She described early childhood as an important opportunity for language learning and actively sought immersion and community resources for her daughter.

Other parents described bilingualism as important for maintaining relationships with relatives, participating in cultural practices, and ensuring that children retained access to family histories and identities.
These aspirations were often informed by participants' own observations of language shift.
During one discussion, an adult participant contrasted his own Spanish with that of his nephew, who used relatively little Spanish beyond words such as "abuelita."
He also described how the child's grandmother eventually began responding in English.
His account framed language shift not as an abstract generational process but as something visible within family relationships.
In this context, participants' efforts to create additional opportunities for Spanish use reflected a desire to interrupt or slow patterns they had observed within their own families.
Aspirational capital therefore intersected with familial and navigational capital.

Participants translated these aspirations into efforts to expand opportunities for language use through home practices, educational programs, cultural activities, family relationships, and their own continued Spanish development.

Aspirational capital operated not simply as a positive orientation toward bilingualism but as a future-oriented resource that motivated participants to seek, create, and navigate opportunities for intergenerational language use.
Participants' accounts also revealed tension between maintaining Spanish and concerns about speaking it "correctly."
Across sessions, correction was not uniformly rejected or embraced.
Instead, families negotiated how to support language growth without discouraging participation.
These tensions were visible in discussions of no sabo forms, correction, and language mixing.
During the first taller, one mother described her children as sometimes using what others might call "no sabo" Spanish.
She rejected ridicule or scolding as a response and instead emphasized encouragement alongside correction.
She recalled her younger child saying "no sabo," after which she taught him to say "no sé."
For her, correction was part of supporting continued development, but it occurred within a broader commitment to keeping the child engaged in Spanish.

Her comparison between her children further illustrated the stakes of this balance: the younger child continued speaking even when unsure, whereas the older child was more likely to remain silent when uncertain.
Similar concerns emerged among young adults.
Two young men described sometimes avoiding Spanish because they were unsure of the "right way" to express themselves.
Their hesitation suggested that opportunities to use the language were shaped not only by proficiency or exposure but also by confidence in whether their Spanish would be judged as acceptable.
At the same time, both described actively trying to create more opportunities to use Spanish, indicating that linguistic insecurity coexisted with a desire to maintain and strengthen the language.
Discussions of language mixing made this tension visible.
Participants shared several expressions that reflected contact between Spanish and English.
One mother recalled her son saying "Ellos querían sorpresarme" [They wanted to surprise me].

Here, sorpresarme appears to be modeled on the English verb surprise; in standardized Spanish, the expected form would be Although excitado is a legitimate Spanish word, in many Spanish varieties it more often conveys heightened arousal, sometimes with a sexual connotation; emocionado would generally be more idiomatic for expressing positive anticipation or excitement.
These examples are consistent with documented English-influenced lexical and semantic patterns in U.S. Spanish (Thomas, 2022).

text.text: The participant recalled that people had laughed at some of these expressions without explaining why they were perceived as inappropriate.

A mother similarly described correcting her children when they used contact-influenced forms, but she emphasized being careful not to overcorrect because she wanted them to continue speaking Spanish and developing their linguistic resources through use.

We interpreted these responses as a form of resistant capital: participants did not necessarily reject correction or standardized Spanish, but they resisted practices that could turn linguistic feedback into shame, silence, or withdrawal from Spanish.
Resistance did not necessarily mean rejecting correction or standardized Spanish.
Rather, it appeared in participants' efforts to resist practices that could turn correction into shame, silence, or withdrawal from the language.
Participants valued expanding children's Spanish while also recognizing that excessive attention to "proper" language could reduce willingness to speak.
This distinction became particularly important because hesitation itself appeared repeatedly across the talleres.
The workshops also revealed that deficit beliefs were not uniformly shared by participants.
During the first session, one mother expressed surprise that bilingualism had ever been viewed as confusing for children; she reported being unfamiliar with that negative belief.
Her response complicated the facilitators' assumption that common bilingualism "myths" would necessarily reflect participants' own concerns.
This contrasting case reinforced the importance of eliciting participants' perspectives before assuming which beliefs or misconceptions were relevant within a particular community.
As part of our aims, we examined how the talleres functioned as spaces for coconstruction and knowledge exchange.
Across sessions, participant contributions did more than illustrate information presented by facilitators.
They introduced new strategies, complicated general recommendations, and at times changed how facilitators framed subsequent discussion.
Case-based activities were useful because participants were asked to respond before facilitators introduced recommendations.
During an early scenario, one child participant suggested associating physical objects with words to help learners connect vocabulary across languages.
In another session, an adult participant drew on his childhood experiences in Tijuana to suggest periods of immersion in Mexico as a strategy for families who had access to crossborder relationships.
These ideas were generated from participants' experiences rather than supplied in advance by the facilitators.

During the final session, a Vietnamese participant argued that understanding a bilingual child's language development required considering the amount of English input and output, time spent using each language at home, and the child's age and grade.
A Japanese mother emphasized cultural responsiveness from teachers when discussing one of the case scenarios.
Such comments redirected discussion from generic bilingualism advice toward the specific relationships and environments in which language development occurred.
Knowledge exchange also took place among participants.
Young adults compared strategies for strengthening Spanish through partners, work, music, and intentional language choices.
Parents compared how different children responded to correction or encouragement.

Discussions of code-switching prompted participants to contribute their own examples, producing shared recognition of language practices that might otherwise be experienced individually as mistakes or sources of embarrassment.
In these moments, the charla format allowed participants to recognize similarities and differences across their experiences rather than positioning the facilitator as the sole source of expertise.
Participant input also shaped our practices.

After the first session, field notes documented that some attendees preferred English or used both English and Spanish, leading the facilitators to consider providing materials in both languages and using more flexible bilingual communication.
By the second session, discussion itself was conducted bilingually and included code-switching and translanguaging.

During the final session, the presence of Vietnamese and Japanese families led us to adapt examples beyond Spanish and to consider how the workshop model could better address multilingual families more broadly.
Library staff similarly encouraged greater attention to languages represented in the surrounding community.
Our reflections also changed in response to participant accounts.
Following discussions of correction and language mixing, notes explicitly emphasized avoiding prescriptivism and moving away from "one size fits all" recommendations.

Participants' descriptions of different children within the same family reinforced the need to frame recommendations as possibilities to be considered in relation to family circumstances rather than universal rules.
Thus, coconstruction occurred not only when participants applied research to their own experiences, but also when their experiences altered how facilitators understood and presented that research.
These interactions positioned the talleres as reciprocal spaces rather than one-way educational presentations.
Participants contributed experiential and contextual knowledge, while facilitators contributed research evidence, structured prompts, and connections to community resources.
Knowledge about bilingual development and heritage-language maintenance was therefore not simply transmitted but interpreted, contextualized, and expanded through dialogue.
Pre-workshop survey responses were available from 19 participants, and 17 participants completed the post-workshop survey.

Responses to the remaining items were largely stable because favorable endorsement was already high at baseline.
On the post-only item, all 17 respondents reported that the taller increased their knowledge of bilingualism.

text.text: The present study examined how participants in community-based bilingualism talleres described the practices and resources they used to support bilingualism and heritage-language maintenance, the forms of Community Cultural Wealth (CCW) reflected in those practices, and the role of the talleres as spaces for knowledge exchange.
Three broader conclusions emerged.

First, heritage-language maintenance was described as a relational and ecological process that extended beyond language use in the home to include extended family, schools, community institutions, cultural activities, workplaces, and transnational connections.
Second, CCW illuminated how participants combined linguistic, familial, social, navigational, aspirational, and resistant resources rather than drawing on these forms of capital independently.
Third, the talleres functioned as reciprocal spaces in which research-based information was interpreted, questioned, and extended through participants lived experiences.

The findings shift attention away from whether families follow a particular language-maintenance strategy and toward the resources, relationships, opportunities, and ideologies that make continued bilingual participation possible.

Our findings suggest that heritage-language maintenance is not sustained through exposure or home-language use alone, but through the accumulation of opportunities to use the language across family, community, educational, and social contexts.

This pattern is consistent with Potowski's (2013) emphasis on intergenerational transmission while also illustrating how transmission is shaped by the broader environments in which families participate.

Rather than relying on a single strategy, participants described maintaining or strengthening Spanish through combinations of home use, literacy, cultural activities, extended-family relationships, schooling, workplaces, community institutions, and social networks.

These findings position heritagelanguage maintenance as an ecological process in which family practices remain central but are strengthened or constrained by the opportunities for meaningful use available beyond the home (Inan & Harris, 2025).
text.formatted: These findings position heritagelanguage maintenance as an ecological process in which family practices remain central but are strengthened or constrained by the opportunities for meaningful use available beyond the home <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Inan & Harris, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The practices participants shared were adaptive rather than fixed.

Participants described different language trajectories even among children raised within the same household, suggesting that family language practices cannot be understood as uniform inputs producing uniform outcomes.
Caregivers continually adjusted their approaches in response to children's confidence, preferences, opportunities for use, and changing environments.
Heritage-language maintenance emerged not simply as the implementation of a family language policy but as an ongoing process of responding to the linguistic ecology of individual family members.

This adaptive pattern is consistent with family language policy research emphasizing that language practices are negotiated within families and shaped by changing relationships, ideologies, and circumstances (Iqwan Sanjani et al., 2026; King et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This adaptive pattern is consistent with family language policy research emphasizing that language practices are negotiated within families and shaped by changing relationships, ideologies, and circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Iqwan Sanjani et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">King et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The border-region context further shaped these opportunities.
Transnational relationships can expand access to Spanish-speaking family members, schooling, literacy practices, and other contexts for language use (Ceballos, 2012).
text.formatted: Transnational relationships can expand access to Spanish-speaking family members, schooling, literacy practices, and other contexts for language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Ceballos, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Participants' experiences similarly suggest that geographic proximity becomes a linguistic resource when families can activate cross-border connections through mobility and relationships.
Proximity alone, however, does not ensure maintenance; access to transnational networks, bilingual schooling, community programs, and Spanish-speaking interlocutors remained uneven.
The border is therefore better understood as part of the opportunity structure surrounding bilingual families than as an inherently protective factor (Potowski, 2013).
text.formatted: The border is therefore better understood as part of the opportunity structure surrounding bilingual families than as an inherently protective factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Potowski, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings also demonstrate that maintenance and shift can occur simultaneously within the same family and community.
Participants recognized changes in Spanish use across generations while also describing deliberate efforts to strengthen their own language use or create opportunities for younger generations.
Heritage-language maintenance should not be understood as a binary outcome in which a family either "maintains" or "loses" a language.
It is a dynamic process shaped by changing relationships, institutions, identities, and opportunities for participation across the lifespan.
Community Cultural Wealth is a useful framework for identifying resources that might remain invisible within deficit-oriented accounts of heritage bilingualism.

A deficit framework could foreground limited access to bilingual education, hesitancy to speak Spanish, contactinfluenced language, or parents' uncertainty about how best to support bilingual development.
Community Cultural Wealth instead directs attention to the knowledge, relationships, strategies, and aspirations families mobilize within those circumstances (Yosso, 2005).
text.formatted: Community Cultural Wealth instead directs attention to the knowledge, relationships, strategies, and aspirations families mobilize within those circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Yosso, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings also support Yosso's (2005) emphasis on the interconnectedness of cultural wealth.
text.formatted: Our findings also support <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Yosso's (2005)</ref> emphasis on the interconnectedness of cultural wealth.

text.text: The forms of capital frequently overlapped: aspirations for intergenerational bilingualism depended on family relationships, linguistic practices, social networks, and the ability to navigate educational and community institutions.
This overlap matters because treating CCW categories too rigidly can obscure how families mobilize multiple resources together.
Community Cultural Wealth is therefore most informative in this context as an interconnected system of resources rather than a checklist of independent forms of capital.
The CCW framework also foregrounds expertise that institutions may overlook.
Participants demonstrated detailed knowledge of their children's language histories, reactions to strategies, family communication patterns, and the opportunities available within their communities.
Young adults similarly drew on knowledge generated through work, relationships, media, and their own histories as bilingual speakers.
These forms of experiential knowledge complicate models in which professionals identify a problem, and families are expected simply to implement a recommended solution.
An asset-based framework should identify family agency without individualizing responsibility for structural conditions.
Families' ability to mobilize cultural wealth depended partly on access to time, transportation, bilingual programs, community institutions, transnational networks, and other resources.
Recognizing family agency therefore does not mean shifting responsibility for heritage-language maintenance entirely onto families.
Rather, CCW makes visible both the resources families possess and the institutional conditions that shape whether those resources can be effectively mobilized.
Yet access to family and community resources does not by itself ensure continued heritage-language use; the social conditions under which speakers use Spanish also matter.
Our findings suggest that efforts to support heritage-language development may discourage participation when linguistic feedback is experienced as a judgment of speaker legitimacy.
Although participants valued helping children expand their Spanish, concerns about speaking "correctly" were also linked to hesitation and reduced participation.

This tension suggests that the consequences of correction depend not simply on whether feedback is provided, but on whether it expands a speaker's repertoire while preserving confidence and willingness to use the language.

In this sense, heritage-language maintenance involves more than developing linguistic knowledge; it also depends on whether speakers experience their bilingual practices as legitimate forms of participation.

This distinction aligns with critiques of deficit frameworks in heritagelanguage research. Higby et al. (2023) argue that bilingual speakers are often evaluated against idealized monolingual norms that do not reflect their histories of language exposure and use.

(2023)</ref> argue that bilingual speakers are often evaluated against idealized monolingual norms that do not reflect their histories of language exposure and use.

text.text: Heritage-language features associated with language contact, bilingual development, or regional variation may consequently be interpreted as evidence of incomplete or deficient competence rather than as products of distinct linguistic experiences.

Concerns about linguistic legitimacy are relevant in Southern California, where Spanish-English bilinguals regularly navigate code-switching, English-influenced forms, and differing expectations about what counts as "proper" Spanish across family, community, and cross-border contexts.
Holguín Mendoza and Higby (2024) show that Southern California bilinguals are aware of the stigma associated with English borrowings, contact forms, and other features of regional Spanish.
text.formatted: Holguín <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Mendoza and Higby (2024)</ref> show that Southern California bilinguals are aware of the stigma associated with English borrowings, contact forms, and other features of regional Spanish.

text.text: At the same time, these forms occur within a recognizable Southern California sociolinguistic system.
Judgments about "proper" Spanish therefore involve more than grammaticality; they also reflect ideologies about which varieties and speakers are granted legitimacy.

A raciolinguistic perspective clarifies why adopting standardized forms does not necessarily resolve this tension. Flores and Rosa (2015) argue that judgments of linguistic appropriateness are shaped by perceptions of speakers as well as by the forms they produce.
text.formatted: A raciolinguistic perspective clarifies why adopting standardized forms does not necessarily resolve this tension. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Flores and Rosa (2015)</ref> argue that judgments of linguistic appropriateness are shaped by perceptions of speakers as well as by the forms they produce.

text.text: Practices associated with bilingualism can be celebrated in some contexts while stigmatized when produced by racialized heritage speakers. Rosa (2016) similarly demonstrates how U.S.

text.text: Latine speakers may be positioned as deficient users of both English and Spanish, producing a condition in which linguistic legitimacy remains difficult to attain even through greater conformity to standardized norms.
Research on linguistic legitimacy and heritage Spanish suggests that supporting heritagelanguage maintenance requires distinguishing between repertoire expansion and linguistic replacement.
Speakers can learn additional lexical, grammatical, or register-specific forms without being taught that their existing bilingual practices are illegitimate.

Instruction and family feedback can therefore emphasize when and where particular forms may be interpreted differently while preserving bilingual variation as part of speakers' communicative resources.
This orientation is consistent with Lynch and Potowski's (2014) critique of prescriptive approaches to U.S. Spanish that prioritize correction over sustained engagement with the heritage language.
text.formatted: This orientation is consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lynch and Potowski's (2014)</ref> critique of prescriptive approaches to U.S. Spanish that prioritize correction over sustained engagement with the heritage language.

text.text: The implications for maintenance are important.
Increasing opportunities to use Spanish may be insufficient if speakers anticipate that participation will expose them to ridicule or judgments about authenticity.

Linguistic legitimacy consequently becomes part of the ecology of language maintenance: speakers need not only opportunities to use the language, but also interactional spaces in which using it is socially viable.

Resistant capital can therefore include challenging deficit interpretations of bilingual practices and sustaining participation despite pressures to conform to narrow definitions of legitimate Spanish.
The importance of linguistic legitimacy also has implications for how bilingual families are engaged in community-based outreach.
Recommendations developed without attention to families lived experiences may reproduce the same prescriptive assumptions that participants were navigating.

Our findings instead support models that recognize families and community members as sources of contextual knowledge about language use, relationships, institutional barriers, and available resources.
The structure of the talleres created opportunities for that knowledge to shape the discussion.

By eliciting participants' interpretations before introducing or finalizing recommendations, research-based information could be considered alongside family and community experience rather than presented as universally applicable guidance.

This reciprocal, dialogic orientation is consistent with community-engaged approaches that position community members as knowledge producers rather than solely as recipients of information (Vaughn et al., 2018) and with Funds of Knowledge perspectives that recognize expertise developed through everyday family and community life (Moll et al., 1992).

text.text: Such reciprocity was important given the linguistic and experiential heterogeneity represented in the workshops.
Participants differed in their relationships to Spanish, other languages, schooling, family networks, and the U.S.-Mexico border.

A dialogic format allowed general research findings to be interpreted within those different circumstances rather than assuming that a single recommendation would be equally appropriate for all families.
Community-based talleres may therefore be most useful when they create structured opportunities for research and community knowledge to inform one another.
The findings have implications for how families, educators, clinicians, and community organizations approach bilingual development and heritage-language maintenance.
Across these settings, a central implication is the need to move away from universal prescriptions.
Families varied in their goals, resources, children's responses to language practices, and access to bilingual opportunities.
Recommendations should therefore provide families with possible strategies and the information needed to evaluate them rather than prescribing a single "best" approach.

Supporting bilingualism may involve home-language use, literacy, cultural activities, educational programs, extended-family relationships, or other opportunities for meaningful interaction, but the usefulness of any strategy depends on the circumstances of the individual family.
For educators and speech-language pathologists, this flexibility also requires distinguishing language support from linguistic correction.
Professionals can help children expand vocabulary, registers, and context-specific forms without treating bilingual or contactinfluenced practices as evidence of inadequate language.

Asking families about children's language histories, communication partners, opportunities for use, and family priorities can provide information that standardized recommendations alone cannot capture.
Clinical and educational guidance should build on families' existing knowledge and practices rather than beginning from assumptions about what families are failing to provide.
Community organizations and libraries can play a complementary role by creating accessible spaces in which families encounter both research-based information and one another.
Our experience also suggests that accessibility involves more than selecting a community location (Cabrera Pérez et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our experience also suggests that accessibility involves more than selecting a community location <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cabrera Pérez et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although interest during outreach and tabling was substantial, workshop attendance remained relatively small.
Community engagement therefore needs to begin before the workshop itself.

Developing relationships with library staff, schools, community organizations, and other trusted local partners may help researchers understand when and how families are most likely to participate, which topics are locally relevant, and how information should be communicated.
Trust and relationship building may be important regardless of whether researchers or professionals are themselves members of the communities in which they work.
Researchers who share cultural, linguistic, or lived experiences with community members may bring valuable insider perspectives, established relationships, and familiarity with local contexts.
However, shared community membership does not automatically ensure trust or eliminate differences in experiences, perspectives, or power.

Similarly, researchers working outside their own communities must be intentional about developing relationships, mutual respect, and recognition of community expertise as foundations of effective academic-community partnerships as the pillars for community-engaged research (Khodyakov et al., 2017; Jagosh et al., 2015).
