text.text: Although the present study did not compare different outreach models, our experience suggests that engagement should begin with relationship building rather than recruitment alone.

Establishing a sustained presence, learning from people already working within the community, and involving trusted community members in outreach and program development may help make communitybased initiatives more locally responsive.
Language accessibility should likewise be responsive rather than assumed in advance.

Although the talleres centered on bilingualism and were initially designed primarily around Spanish, participants differed in the languages they used with facilitators and in the linguistic backgrounds represented within their families.

Future programs could incorporate bilingual materials, flexible use of Spanish and English, and code-switching when appropriate rather than treating one language as the required medium of participation.

The participation of individuals from linguistic backgrounds beyond Spanish-English further suggests that community conversations about bilingualism should remain responsive to the broader multilingual ecology of the community.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
The study involved a small, self-selected group of participants across four talleres.

Individuals who chose to attend workshops focused on bilingualism may have had particular interest in or favorable orientations toward multilingualism that are not representative of the broader community.
Attendance also differed across sessions, and some individuals participated more actively than others.
As a result, themes that appeared across the dataset should not be interpreted as reflecting the prevalence of beliefs or practices within City Heights or bilingual families more generally.
Recruitment and participation provide an additional consideration.
Informal outreach generated considerable interest, but that interest did not consistently translate into workshop attendance.

Because reasons for nonattendance were not systematically collected, the present study cannot determine whether participation was affected by timing, competing responsibilities, outreach methods, topic relevance, or other factors.

Future community-partnered work could examine recruitment and participation more systematically and involve local organizations and community members earlier in decisions about scheduling, format, language, and content.
The qualitative dataset relied on our field notes rather than complete audio recordings and verbatim transcripts of workshop discussions.
Field notes allowed us to document participant experiences, examples, questions, and facilitator reflections, but they inevitably represent a selective record of interaction.
They may not capture the full wording, sequence, or complexity of participants' contributions.

Moreover, because we also documented and analyzed the workshop interactions, the field notes and interpretations were necessarily shaped by what we noticed and considered salient during and after each session.
Collaborative review, analytic memoing, and attention to discrepant cases were used to strengthen reflexivity and credibility, but these procedures do not eliminate our interpretive role.
For this reason, interpretations in the present study focus on recurring patterns across the documented discussions rather than detailed discourse-level analysis.

Future studies could combine field notes with audio-recorded and transcribed discussions, participant reflections, or follow-up interviews to preserve more of the interactional context and participants' own language.
The survey findings should also be interpreted cautiously.
The survey was brief, several items showed high favorable endorsement at baseline, item-level responses were missing for some participants, and role-specific items resulted in different denominators.
As mentioned in an earlier section, the observed pre-post differences are best understood as descriptive patterns in participants' responses rather than as evidence of workshop effectiveness.

Future studies could use larger samples, validated measures, and longitudinal designs to examine whether participation in community-based bilingualism workshops is associated with sustained changes in knowledge, beliefs, or practices.
The workshops included participants with heterogeneous linguistic, generational, educational, and family backgrounds.

This heterogeneity enriched the discussions and was central to the co-constructive character of the talleres, but the small sample does not permit meaningful comparisons among particular linguistic or demographic groups.
Future research could examine how community-based bilingualism initiatives operate across different heritagelanguage communities while retaining attention to local linguistic and cultural conditions.
Heritage-language maintenance depends on more than families' desire to raise bilingual children.

It is shaped by the opportunities speakers have to use their languages across relationships and settings, their access to educational and community resources, and whether their bilingual practices are treated as legitimate forms of communication.

Families in the present study already drew on linguistic, familial, social, navigational, aspirational, and resistant resources to create and sustain such opportunities, often while navigating unequal access to institutional support and competing ideas about what counts as "proper" language.
Community-based spaces can support this work when they recognize those resources rather than positioning families as recipients of expert solutions.

The talleres showed how research evidence can be brought into dialogue with family experience, local knowledge, and community resources, producing conversations that are more responsive to the realities of bilingual life.

These findings suggest that supporting heritage-language maintenance involves not only sharing research on bilingual development but also creating structures through which families and communities can shape how that knowledge is interpreted and applied.
